name: PT IMC Pelita Logistik Tbk

frontmatter.title: IMC Pelita Logistik - net cash cannot fix a sub-cost-of-capital fleet
frontmatter.summary: IMC Pelita Logistik moves coal and dry bulk on owned tugs, barges and floating loading facilities. The downcycle is real, the balance sheet is net cash, and the stock trades below book. But the fleet earns a low return on capital even after our margin recovery, the final shipping levy and a full replacement-capex charge cut free cash flow, and the market already discounts a much faster recovery than we forecast. We move to SELL.
thesis: PSSI is a shipping operator, not a coal trader or a miner: it is paid to move tonnes, so the economic drivers are fleet utilisation and tariffs, not the price of the cargo it carries [S2].

The downcycle is real but it was a volume cycle, not a tariff collapse: volume fell from 21.0 Mt in FY2024 to 14.0 Mt in FY2025 while revenue per tonne rose, and nine-month 2026 revenue of US$35.1m was below the US$44.5m earned a year earlier [S2, S3, F1, F2].

The balance sheet is the floor: at September 2026 the company held US$56.4m of cash and deposits and US$7.5m of financial assets against US$14.2m of bank loans, and the fleet's net book value was US$80.1m [S3].
The floor is not the value: book equity of US$150.2m earns a forecast ROE of 1.9% by FY2030E, and the DCF at a full replacement-capex charge gives Rp258 against the Rp336 price [S0, S3].

The weighted target is Rp244, -27.3% below the last close, but the probability-weighted value before the fund's 20.0% ADTV haircut is Rp306 against the Rp336 price: the haircut, not the operating forecast, is what separates SELL from HOLD [S0].

catalysts.event: Recording date for the treasury-share bonus (ex-date 6 November 2026); distribution on 27 November 2026
2027 RKAB quota approval, the main swing factor for customer coal volumes and barge demand
FY2026 audited results; watch the full-year gross margin against the nine-month run-rate and the capex peak
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision under the stated payout policy
Staged delivery of the six renewal vessels and first disclosure of their utilisation

blocks.text: **Rating SELL · target Rp244 · last close Rp336 · return -27.3%**

**Undiscounted expected return Rp306 against the Rp336 close: a negative return inside the HOLD band, so on the fundamentals alone this is a HOLD. The Rp244 target and the SELL rating are the constitution's 20.0% ADTV haircut applied to that value, shown as its own line [S0].**

**What changed.** The published view was REDUCE; it becomes SELL because the own-history EV/EBITDA cross-check is now zero-weighted. That multiple was computed on FY2022-FY2024 data-pack EBITDA whose depreciation is a fraction of the true charge, so it inflated the blend and its removal is a correction of a known-stale input, not a change of view [S0, S2]. The fuel pass-through is now measured rather than asserted: fuel intensity rose on the nine-month revenue base towards the US$9.4m of fuel cost, while Brent rose by roughly two-fifths, so we cut the modelled pass-through from most of a move to part of one [S3, F58, F59, F60]. The bear case now carries a renewal-capex shock, so a delivery slip cuts the operating case and the cash bridge together [S5].

**The liquidity haircut is disclosed, not hidden.** The target of Rp244 and the SELL rating are produced by applying the constitution's 20.0% ADTV haircut to the undiscounted value, because PSSI trades IDR127.8m a day against a free float of 16.2% [S0]. The haircut is a fund exit constraint, not a second estimate of the stock's price: it measures what our own position can be sold for in this tape, is applied on the same ladder to every name below the fund's liquidity floor, and is shown as its own line rather than folded into the discount rate. It is not double counting of the stock's illiquidity, but it is the single largest reason the rating is SELL rather than HOLD, and a reader should weigh the undiscounted value above with that in mind.

**Bonus-share basis, at today's ex-date.** The one-for-thirty treasury-share bonus approved at the 28 October 2026 RUPS went ex on 6 November 2026; the record date is 9 November 2026 and the shares are distributed on 27 November 2026 [S9]. It transfers 172.0m treasury shares to holders on top of the 5,161m distribution base, so the post-bonus count is those two together and every holder's percentage is unchanged; the Rp17.2bn headline is the nominal value charged to additional paid-in capital inside equity, a reclassification and not a cash return [S9, S7, F27, F38, F41, F57]. Because the last close of Rp336 is the 5 November cum-bonus price, every per-share figure in this note — target, EPS, DPS and book value — is struck on the 5,161m cum-bonus count, the same basis as the price; on the post-bonus count the per-share figures are proportionately lower and the return is unchanged, because the bonus creates no value [S0, S9, F38, F41]. The Kontan report of the disclosure prints a one-for-one ratio [S9]; that contradicts the same report's own 172.0m share figure and the thirty-to-one ratio in the IDX Channel report [S6], and a one-for-one bonus would need more shares than the company holds in treasury [F42], so we use the thirty-to-one ratio [S6, S7, S9, F27, F41, F42].

On that single share and price basis, this revision changes the valuation, not the business description. We have dropped the P/BV cross-check because the own-history book multiple was struck when ROE was near its cycle peak, charged the final shipping levy through operating costs, lifted long-run capex to the depreciation charge, and restated the balance sheet to 30 September 2026. The cumulative effect is a lower target and a change of rating from the published REDUCE to SELL [S0, S3, S7, F38, F40].

The company is still in the trough of its cycle. Revenue fell from US$102.4m in FY2023 to US$57.1m in FY2025, and the nine months to September 2026 produced US$35.1m against US$44.5m a year earlier [S0, S3]. The decline was volume-led: cargo volume fell from 21.0 Mt to 14.0 Mt, while revenue per tonne rose, so the earlier statement that volumes and tariffs both fell was wrong and is corrected here [S2, F1, F2]. The FY2025 net profit was US$0.2m, down from US$14.2m, and the net result for the first nine months of 2026 was US$-0.8m, a loss [S0, S3].

The variant view is not that the cycle is about to boom; it is that the market is already paying for a faster recovery than the fleet's economics support. At the cum-bonus Rp336 close the equity is worth IDR1.73tn, and cash, deposits and financial assets net of bank loans are more than half of that market value, while cash, funds and the fleet's net book value together exceed it; the asset backing is the real support [S3, S0, F56]. But the operating business earns a low return on that capital: the DCF gives Rp258 a share, and the market-implied FY2027E revenue growth of 16.6% is far above our 5.0% [S0]. The asset backing limits how far the shares should fall, not whether they are too high today.

What moves the value, in order: the tariff and utilisation recovery as the oversupplied barge market absorbs capacity; the fleet-renewal programme and whether the new barges earn a return above their cost; and the pace at which the large net cash position is returned to shareholders or reinvested [S2, S5]. The dividend is small at the trough, and the stated policy caps distribution at a share of net profit, so the cash is not automatically a shareholder return [S2].

Coal barge operators sit between the mine and the export terminal or power plant. They load at a jetty or transshipment anchorage, carry the cargo downriver or along the coast, and transfer it to a mother vessel or unload it at a port. The business is asset-heavy and operationally geared: a barge earns money only when it is moving, so utilisation and the freight rate per tonne matter far more than the coal price itself. In a tight fleet market tariffs rise and older tonnage is sold at a gain; in an oversupplied market tariffs fall faster than costs, and the operator absorbs the difference. The balance sheet, the age profile of the fleet and the contract book are therefore the things to watch through a cycle.

PT IMC Pelita Logistik Tbk was founded in 2007, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2017 and changed its name from PT Pelita Samudera Shipping Tbk in February 2023 [S2]. It describes itself as a maritime shipping and integrated logistics company providing transshipment, inter-island and international dry-bulk transportation, with a primary focus on the coal mining supply chain [S2]. Its fleet at the end of FY2024 numbered 52 vessels and at the end of FY2025 48, as older tonnage was sold; it operated 47 vessels at September 2026 before the new-build programme [S2, S5, F8, F28, F53].

The revenue mix is a shipping mix. In FY2025 floating loading and freight earned US$38.0m, time charter earned US$16.9m, the bunker adjustment added US$1.2m, and demurrage, warehouse rental and other services made up the remainder, for total revenue of US$57.1m [S2]. The company runs a deliberate balance between medium-term time-charter and freight-charter contracts and selective spot work, which management says gives revenue visibility while preserving flexibility [S2]. It does not disclose contract lengths, day rates or a backlog, so the visibility is asserted rather than quantified; we treat the contract book as real but thin evidence.

Customers are coal miners, shippers and industrial buyers. The notes single out only one customer above the disclosure threshold, PT Samudera Nusa Perkasa, at US$5.7m of sales in FY2025, which is a low concentration for an Indonesian coal-logistics name and a genuine positive [S2]. The customer names behind the rest of the book are not disclosed. The company does not name its largest customers, so we cannot test renewal risk customer by customer; the annual report's claim of long-term relationships is the only evidence [S2].

Strategy as management frames it has several parts: keep fleet utilisation high through route and schedule adjustments; strengthen the contract portfolio by balancing time charter and spot; and develop an integrated logistics platform through warehouse assets and the OLI, OKI and PSP entities in Karawang [S2]. The integrated-logistics initiative is early stage, with limited contribution to date, and the company says so [S2]. The more material capital decision is the fleet renewal: new tugs and barges have been ordered at Batam yards, with each new barge carrying more than 10,000 tonnes, and delivery staged according to market conditions [S5]. Management frames it as reliability and flexibility for customers rather than as capacity growth, which is consistent with a replacement programme in an oversupplied market [S5].

Control is concentrated. PT Indoprima Marine held 43.8% of the issued shares at the end of FY2025, and PT Himpunan Primajaya is the controlling party of Indoprima Marine and the ultimate controlling shareholder [S2]. The public free float is 16.2%, thin enough that the house applies a liquidity discount to the valuation [S0]. The company is distributing 172.0m treasury shares as a bonus at a ratio of one new share for every 30 held; because the shares come from treasury and the distribution is pro rata, total issued shares are unchanged and no holder's percentage changes. The Rp17.2bn headline figure is the nominal value of the shares transferred out of additional paid-in capital, not a cash return, so total equity does not move. The press reports of the controlling and public stakes rising are an arithmetic error from applying the bonus ratio to the percentage rather than to the share count, and we do not repeat them [S6, S7, S9, F27, F41, F57]. The company employs 105 people directly, which is consistent with an outsourced-crew, asset-owning model [S0].

The group structure is a parent with operating subsidiaries for sea freight, property and the new logistics entities; the company reports no bonds, sukuk or convertible securities outstanding at the end of FY2025 [S2]. That simplicity is a governance positive: the capital structure is bank debt and leases, not layered securities with conversion or coupon risk.

The industry is Indonesian coal distribution and maritime logistics. The annual report frames it through the domestic market obligation: coal remained the main source of national power generation, domestic obligation supply reached a large share of national output, and most production was still exported, so the movement from mine to port and from port to buyer is a permanent need [S2]. The coal deck we carry prices the seaborne market, and its path runs from US$137/t in FY2026E to US$118/t in FY2027E and US$105/t in the long run, with spot at US$150/t [deck]. For a barge operator the absolute price matters less than the volume it implies and the tariff the fleet can charge; a lower coal price that keeps Indonesian volumes steady is not bad for PSSI, and a price spike that curtails customer production is not good. The deck is context for the revenue path rather than a mechanical driver: the industry template takes revenue from our growth assumption, and we set that assumption against the deck's implied coal trade rather than the deck entering revenue directly. The corporate template's coal cost link is switched off because coal is cargo, not an input, so if the link were live the variable that would enter is d.coal.newc through a volume share — the Newcastle price itself never touches our revenue line [S2, deck].

The direct commodity cost is fuel. Marine diesel and fuel oil cost US$12.2m in FY2025, a material share of cost of revenue of US$51.6m, and the oil deck's Brent path runs from US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E to US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E [S2, deck]. The company recovers part of a fuel move through tariff resets, and the evidence is not flattering: in the nine months to September 2026 fuel of US$9.4m was a larger share of revenue than a year earlier, so the cost base did not shrink in step with revenue and fuel intensity rose rather than normalised [S3, F60]. We therefore model a partial pass-through rather than a full one, and a sustained oil spike compresses the spread, which is why the bear case carries a lower margin [S2, S3].

Regulation shapes the business in three ways. First, RKAB production quotas govern how much coal the customers can mine, and therefore how many tonnes they need moved; management explicitly cites RKAB uncertainty as a cause of the volume decline [S2]. Second, the domestic market obligation and the price cap on domestic-power coal affect where coal flows and which logistics routes are busy [S2]. Third, shipping income is taxed through a final levy on vessel-operation and charter revenue at a rate of 1.2%, plus corporate income tax on the residual; the levy is charged even when the pre-levy result is a loss, which is why the trough tax line is not zero and why we model it explicitly [S2, S3, F43, F52]. We do not model a royalty or a mining tax because the company has none [S2].

Competition is fragmented and the fleet is oversupplied. The annual report says fleet supply was relatively high in the market and that this affected freight rates and vessel utilisation, which is the clearest statement of the competitive problem [S2]. Barriers to entry are capital and contracts rather than geology: a new entrant can buy or charter barges, but it needs customer relationships, port access and a safety record. PSSI's position is that of a mid-sized, long-established operator with a mixed fleet and a diversified customer list, not the largest and not a price-setter. Its moat is the fleet's suitability for shallow-draft river and transshipment work, the switching cost of integrating a barge schedule into a mine's export chain, and a customer base that is less concentrated than the sector norm [S2].

The five forces are mixed. Buyer power is moderate: the disclosed customer concentration is low, but coal miners and traders are sophisticated and can re-tender, and the customer is larger than the operator in most cases [S2]. Supplier power is low: shipyards, crew, fuel and spare parts are available from many sources. New entrants are a real threat in an oversupplied market, because additional barges can be chartered in. Substitutes are the energy transition and the substitution of rail or truck haulage for short coastal moves, both slow within our horizon. Rivalry is high on price and utilisation, and the industry's returns depend on fleet discipline, which is exactly what the downcycle has tested.

The company's own fleet data show the operating leverage. Tug-and-barge utilisation was 94.0% in FY2025, while floating loading facilities ran lower and motor vessels lower still [S2]. A high utilisation rate on a falling revenue base means the tariff, not the idle time, did the damage; that is consistent with the company's account of oversupply and price pressure [S2]. The renewal programme is a bet that newer, larger barges will win the work that is available on better terms, and it is the single largest discretionary capital commitment in the forecast [S5].

The revenue history is a full cycle compressed into a few lines. Revenue fell from US$119.3m in FY2022 to US$102.4m, US$81.2m and US$57.1m, a cumulative decline driven first by the coal-price correction and then by volume pressure [S0, S2]. Volume fell from 21.0 Mt in FY2024 to 14.0 Mt in FY2025, while revenue per tonne rose as tariffs reset; that is the more accurate reading of the downcycle, and it matters because a volume-led trough can recover with coal output even if tariffs stay flat [S2, F1, F2, F30]. Gross margin moved from 36.3% to 36.8%, 26.1% and 9.6%, and EBITDA margin, restated for the true depreciation charge, moved from 31.5% to 21.3% [S0, S2]. Net profit to parent fell from US$42.2m to US$0.2m [S0].

Revenue per vessel is the test the red team set and the model passes it only partly. The fleet went from 52 vessels at end-FY2024 to 48 at end-FY2025 and 47 at September 2026 as older tonnage was sold, while the six new tugs and barges are a renewal of that capacity, not an addition: the fleet count rises to roughly 48 plus the new deliveries, and management describes them as reliability and flexibility rather than capacity growth [S2, S5, F8, F28]. We therefore do not add their revenue on top of the existing fleet, which is why the revenue path grows by single digits against a larger hull count and unit revenue stays below the FY2025 level. The retirement schedule and the tariff per tonne are not disclosed, so this is a judgement, not a sourced number; a renewed, larger barge should earn at or above the legacy rate once utilisation normalises, and the bull case is where that shows up. A reader who believes the new barges earn the legacy unit revenue should hold the bull case, not the base.

The data pack materially understates depreciation, and we restate it. The pack shows a token FY2025 D&A charge, while the fixed-asset note of the audited accounts reports US$12.8m of fixed-asset depreciation charged to profit or loss, part in cost of revenue and part in operating expenses [S2]. FY2024 was US$15.0m [S2]. We use the filing's figures for both years, which lifts historical EBITDA from the pack's near-zero print to a positive number and changes every margin and multiple built on it; this is a restatement of wrong data, not a modelling choice [S2].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. In FY2025 cost of revenue of US$51.6m comprised depreciation, US$12.2m of fuel, US$8.3m of charter hire, and the remainder in spare parts, vessel operations, crew, repairs, port charges and insurance [S2]. Operating expenses were US$6.1m, including US$1.3m of directors' fees, which is a high charge for a company of this size and a governance point we return to in section six [S2]. Because a large share of the cost base is fixed in the short run, a fall in revenue hits gross profit disproportionately, and the FY2025 gross margin of 9.6% is the result [S2].

Charter hire is the largest single move in the interim accounts and the report was missing it. It fell to US$3.0m in the nine months to September 2026 from US$6.5m a year earlier, a halving that annualises to about two-fifths below the US$8.3m FY2025 charge and is worth several points of gross margin on the FY2026E revenue base [S3, F21, F58, F59]. We read it as structural rather than cyclical: the cost line falls with chartered-in tonnage, and the company has been selling older vessels and taking delivery of owned new-builds, so a restored fleet needs less hired capacity to move the same cargo [S2, S5]. That is why the base case recovers gross margin from the nine-month trough to 19.0% by FY2030E on a partly fixed owned-fleet cost base, and why we do not carry the FY2025 charter line forward. The risk is the mirror image: if the cut reflects the volume decline and the hired tonnage returns with the 2027 RKAB cycle, the margin path is too generous, which is the bear case [S3].

The nine months to September 2026 show the trough. Revenue was US$35.1m against US$44.5m, gross profit was US$3.6m, and the net result was US$-0.8m, a loss [S3]. The interim accounts report the nine-month aggregate and carry no quarterly split, so we do not read a sequential recovery or a sequential decline into them; the FY2026E forecast is set from the nine-month actual annualised plus a small fourth-quarter uplift, not from a single quarter extrapolated [S3].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual at last year's economics and then lets the cycle recover modestly. FY2026E revenue is US$48.0m, a growth rate of -16.0% on the nine-month run-rate, with a gross margin of 8.7% and EBITDA of US$8.9m [S0, S3]. The FY2026E revenue is below FY2025 because the nine-month actual is below the prior year; the margin is close to the last actual once the final shipping levy, which we charge through operating costs, is added back, and the like-for-like comparison is disclosed in the operating-cost paragraph below [S2, S3]. Revenue then grows as the new vessels join the fleet, and the gross margin recovers to 19.0% by FY2030E, still below the 26.1% achieved in FY2024 and far below the FY2023 peak [S2]. The recovery is operating leverage on a partly fixed fleet cost base, not a return to the boom.

The recovery is deliberately not a flat-COGS assumption. Fuel and charter hire are variable with volume and together are a material share of cost of revenue, so a revenue path driven by new vessels carries incremental fuel and charter cost; we let roughly two-fifths of the cost base flex with volume, which produces the margin path above rather than holding absolute COGS flat while revenue grows [S2, F20, F21]. The earlier terminal margin was delivered by flat absolute COGS and is not supported by the evidence; the new path is lower but still well above the nine-month trough [S2, S3].

The final shipping levy is a real cash cost at the trough. The company pays a 1.2% final tax on vessel-operation and charter revenue, and the nine-month 2026 charge was US$0.3m even though the pre-final-tax result was a loss [S3, F43, F52]. Because the engine's free-cash-flow formula carries only a profit tax, we include the levy in operating costs, which is why the reported opex ratio rises to 11.7% and why forecast EBITDA is after the levy and not directly comparable with the pre-levy historical print [S3, F43]. Corporate income tax at the statutory rate then applies to the residual; the combined burden reconciles to the nine-month run-rate [S3, F52].

Capital expenditure is the swing factor in the near term. The company spent US$9.6m on fixed assets in FY2025 but US$15.6m in the nine months to September 2026 as the renewal programme was paid for [S2, S3]. We carry capex at 40.0% of revenue in FY2026E, falling to 20.0% in FY2027E and the FY2025 actual 17.0% through FY2030E while the renewed fleet is young; from FY2031E the long-run ratio rises to the depreciation charge of 21.5% [S2, S3, S5]. The earlier assumption held capex at 17.0% in perpetuity, which added roughly two-fifths of terminal free cash flow from under-investment; we do not keep that [S2, S3]. The consequence is a negative free cash flow year in FY2026E and a return to positive free cash flow from FY2027E; the DCF discounts that profile rather than ignoring it.

Working capital is modest and positive. Operating working capital was US$6.5m, about 11.0% of revenue, and the September 2026 balance sheet shows the same order of magnitude in receivables, contract assets, inventories and payables [S2, S3]. Trade receivables of US$5.2m against revenue of US$57.1m is a low receivables ratio for Indonesia, and the company's customer base is diversified; the earnings-quality screen does not fire on receivables growth [S0, S2]. Operating cash flow was US$14.4m in FY2025 and US$7.2m in the nine months to September 2026, comfortably above net profit in both periods, so accruals are clean [S0, S3].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case, and it is current to September. The company held US$49.4m of cash, US$7.0m of time deposits and US$7.5m of financial assets at fair value, against US$3.4m of current and US$10.8m of non-current bank borrowings plus small lease liabilities [S3]. Equity attributable to the parent was US$150.2m at September 2026, and the fleet's net book value was US$80.1m, up from the December 2025 figure as the renewal capex landed [S3, F39, F45]. The bank debt is a term loan from PT Bank Multiarta Sentosa secured on fixed assets, with a debt-service covenant disclosed in the loan note [S3]. The forecast in the model builds its opening debt from the audited December 2025 balance sheet, while the valuation bridge is struck on the 30 September 2026 actual, where the term loan has been drawn down further; the bridge is what the target uses, so the projected net-cash line in the table runs ahead of the reconciled September net cash by the amount of that drawdown. We state the gap rather than leave a reader to find it [S3, F46, F47]. Net cash, not net debt, is the right frame for this company, and the valuation bridge uses the September figures rather than the June data pack [S3].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but inconsistent. The company paid a dividend of US$1.4m out of FY2025 profit and has paid above its stated cap in stronger years: the payout ratio was 41.0% for FY2022, 40.0% for FY2023 and a 95.0% interim for FY2024 [S2, F25, F49, F50, F51]. The stated policy is to distribute up to a maximum share of net profit, so the dividend is discretionary and the cash balance is not a committed return [S2, F26]. The renewal programme is the competing use of cash, and we treat the capex as ordered rather than committed because delivery is staged subject to market and yard conditions [S5]. The buyback and the bonus issue are covered in section six.

Earnings-quality flags are limited but worth stating. Accruals are clean: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025 and in the first nine months of 2026 [S0, S3]. Revenue concentration is low by the standards of the sector, with a single disclosed customer singled out by size [S2]. The unusual items are the bargain-purchase gain and asset-sale gains in FY2025, which flatter the reported pre-tax profit but are not in our EBITDA or cash-flow forecast [S2]. The high directors' fee line and the related-party arrangements are governance, not accounting, flags [S2, S3]. We could not verify the exchange's board notation or surveillance status from a primary announcement in this window; we do not use it as a valuation input, and we note the evidence as thin [S0].

We value PSSI on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, because the company is worth the tariffs it earns on tonnes and the cash it converts, not a reserve in the ground. The DCF carries the whole weight and the own-history EV/EBITDA cross-check is zero-weighted. We have dropped P/BV entirely. A book multiple is not a value anchor for this earnings path: the own-history P/BV average spans the 2022-23 boom, when ROE was near its cycle peak, as well as the 2025 trough, while our forecast ROE is -0.7% in the first forecast year and 1.9% by FY2030E, and the ROE-justified book multiple at that return is far below the own-history level. Keeping P/BV at a weight would have added value the forecast does not earn [S0, S2, S3].

The cost of capital is a US-dollar build, because the company reports in dollars. The risk-free rate is 4.8%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, and the levered beta 1.12 on a modest debt weight of 13.0%, giving a cost of equity of 12.3%. With pre-tax debt at 6.8% and the statutory tax rate, the weighted average cost of capital is 11.4% [S0]. Terminal growth is the house US-dollar rate of 2.0%.

The DCF produces Rp258 a share, with the terminal value at 47.1% of the total. The cash flows that support it are the demonstrated ones: a gross margin that troughs near the nine-month 2026 level and recovers to 19.0% by FY2030E, capex that peaks with the renewal, settles at the FY2025 ratio while the fleet is young and then rises to the depreciation charge in the long run, and a net cash balance that is added to the enterprise value [S2, S3, S5]. The single most important assumption is the margin recovery; the sensitivity table shows what happens if it does not arrive. The terminal value is not the majority of the value, so the DCF is not a perpetual-growth artefact: the explicit forecast carries the larger share [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check sits above the DCF and we now give it no weight, because the multiple is a known-stale input rather than a second opinion. The own-history mid-single-digit multiple is computed on data-pack EBITDA that understated the depreciation charge in FY2022 and FY2023 as well as FY2024 and FY2025; those years' D&A in the pack is a fraction of the charge on PP&E above a hundred million dollars, so their EBITDA was understated and the multiples struck on them were overstated [S0, S2]. Restating the earlier years needs filings we do not hold in this window, and a cross-check we know to be wrong cannot carry any of the blend. We therefore report it, flag the direction of the error and let the DCF stand alone. The peer screen is not a substitute: the five covered coal-logistics peers range from single-digit to distressed and speculative multiples, the full screen's median is far from PSSI's own multiple, and the closest comparable names trade near PSSI's trough multiple. We therefore do not use a peer median [S0]. The probability-weighted scenario value before the liquidity discount is Rp306; after the 20.0% discount, which is the constitution's ADTV ladder for a stock trading IDR127.8m a day and not an analyst choice, the target is Rp244 [S0]. That haircut is a fund exit constraint applied across the whole book, not a second estimate of the stock's own illiquidity: the Rp336 close already reflects what the marginal buyer will pay for a 16.2% float, whereas the haircut reflects what a position of our size can be sold for [S0]. The target and the Rp336 close are both quoted per cum-bonus share, on the 5,161m count; after the 6 November 2026 ex-date the same economics are struck per post-bonus share, so the return of -27.3% does not change with the bonus [S7, F38]. The EV-to-equity bridge counts the US$7.5m non-operating line as financial assets at fair value through profit or loss, which is what the balance sheet reports — the company holds no associates of material size — adds the US$56.4m of cash and deposits, deducts the US$14.2m of bank loans and the small non-controlling interest, and excludes the current and non-current lease liabilities disclosed in the lease note; that omission is immaterial at the share level [S3, F46, F47, F48].

What does today's price imply? We invert the model on FY2027E revenue growth: at Rp336 the market is paying for revenue growth of 16.6% in FY2027E against the 5.0% we forecast, holding the discount rate, terminal growth and margin path at our assumptions [S0]. The market is not pricing a flat-to-slowly-recovering business, as the earlier draft claimed; it is pricing a recovery roughly three times faster than our base. That is the variant view: the net cash and the asset backing are real, but they are already in the price, and the operating business does not earn its cost of capital at the returns we can source, so the undiscounted value sits below the close. The step from that to SELL is the liquidity haircut described above, and the rating should be read that way [S0, S3].

The dividend-capacity anchor is the balance sheet, not the dividend. At the policy cap the regular dividend on a depressed net profit is negligible, but the company has distributed above the cap in stronger years, with payout ratios of 41.0%, 40.0% and 95.0% in the three prior periods [S2, F49, F50, F51]. A special dividend or buyback of part of the net cash is a plausible use of the balance sheet, and it is the main upside risk to our target, described in section five. It does not add value in our arithmetic, and we say so rather than counting it twice: the net cash is already inside the bridge at face value, so paying it out moves value from the company to the holder and leaves the total unchanged. A buyback at the Rp336 close would be executed above our intrinsic value and would therefore be mildly dilutive to continuing holders, not accretive; only a buyback below intrinsic adds value. The board has shown willingness to exceed the policy cap, but the family controls the distribution decision and there is no commitment [S2, S3]. The market's anchor is asset value and net cash, not dividend yield, and on that anchor the shares are not cheap enough to compensate for the sub-cost-of-capital operating return [S0, S3].
The downside risks are cyclical, operational and governance-related, in that order.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | What we watch | |---|---|---|---| | Tariffs stay depressed as the barge fleet remains oversupplied | High | High | Quarterly revenue per unit and the company's own commentary on fleet supply [S2, S3] | | RKAB quotas or customer production cut coal volumes | High | High | 2027 quota approvals and customer shipment guidance [S2] | | Final shipping levy and corporate tax take a larger share at trough margins | High | Medium | The final-tax note and the income-tax reconciliation in each LK [S3] | | Fuel and charter costs outrun tariff resets | Medium | Medium | Gross margin against the oil deck and the fuel line in each LK [S2, S3] | | Renewal capex extends into FY2027 or FY2028, or new vessels fail to fill | Medium | High | Delivery schedule, capex cash flow and utilisation disclosures [S5] | | Customer concentration | Low to medium | Medium | The annual customer disclosure; a single customer is singled out by size [S2] | | Governance: high directors' fees, related-party payables, thin float | Medium | Medium | Related-party note and board remuneration each year [S2, S3] | | Liquidity: tiny free float and low traded value | High | Medium | Free float, traded value and any exchange announcement [S0] | | Coal demand erosion from the energy transition | Low within the horizon | High beyond it | PLN generation mix and the domestic obligation policy [S2] |

The bear case holds the company in the downcycle: tariffs stay flat, the new vessels arrive late or do not fill so the renewal slips and the group carries the old and new fleet at once, fuel stays high enough to eat the spread, and the fleet earns below its cost of capital through the forecast. It applies a lower revenue path, a lower margin, a higher capex charge and a higher cost of capital, and it gives Rp199 before the liquidity discount, below the base but still above the net-cash floor because the balance sheet cannot be spent twice [S3]. The base case recovers to mid-cycle margins below the prior peak and gives Rp289. The bull case assumes a faster tariff recovery, a fuller fleet, delivery at contracted prices and a partial re-rating of the multiple as free cash flow turns, and gives Rp505. Probabilities are 30.0% bear, 50.0% base and 20.0% bull. The four shocks are mirrored, but the value outcomes are not, and the reason is arithmetic rather than an extra bull assumption: at a trough gross margin the margin shock is a far larger proportional move in EBITDA and free cash flow than the same shock applied to a recovered margin, and the DCF's operating leverage on a fleet whose capex is close to its EBITDA amplifies that difference in both directions; the net cash bridge truncates the downside at the value of cash it holds. We keep the mirrored shocks rather than fit them to a symmetric answer [S0, S3].

The signposts that would change our view: a sustained rise in the quarterly gross margin above the nine-month 2026 level would say the tariff cycle has turned and would move us toward the bull case; a resumption of the revenue decline after the nine-month stabilisation would say the trough is deeper; a decision to return the excess cash through a special dividend or a larger regular payout would compress the discount to book and is the clearest upside catalyst; and any related-party transaction of size or a change in the renewal budget would raise the governance discount [S2, S3]. A delivery schedule that shows the renewal complete and a utilisation rate at or above the FY2025 level would support the capex thesis; an extension of the programme into FY2027 would delay the free-cash-flow turn [S5].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Indoprima Marine held 43.8% of the issued shares at the end of FY2025, and PT Himpunan Primajaya controls Indoprima Marine and is the ultimate controlling shareholder [S2]. The public free float is 16.2%, just above the exchange's minimum, and the stock's traded value is thin enough that the house applies a liquidity discount [S0]. The ownership is a single family-linked group rather than a multi-entity conglomerate, and we treat it as a standard controlling-shareholder structure [S2]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the annual report; the only security disclosed is the mortgage over fixed assets for the bank term loan [S2].

The bonus issue does not change control. The company is distributing 172.0m treasury shares at a ratio of one bonus share for every 30 held, with a cum date of 5 November 2026, an ex date of 6 November 2026, a recording date of 9 November 2026 and distribution on 27 November 2026, charged to additional paid-in capital so total equity is unchanged; because the shares come from treasury and the distribution is pro rata, total issued shares are unchanged and every holder's percentage is unchanged [S7, F27, F41]. The press reports that the controlling stake rises from 43.8% to a higher figure and the public float rises alongside it are arithmetically wrong: multiplying a percentage by the bonus ratio ignores that the bonus is a transfer, not a new issue, and the freed-up float is a distribution of existing treasury shares, not a change in the ownership split [S6, S7, S9]. We keep the ownership percentages unchanged. Every per-share figure uses the 5,161m shares outstanding on the cum-bonus distribution base, which is the count the quoted price is struck on; after the ex-date the same economics apply to the larger post-bonus count, with the target per share proportionately lower and the return unchanged, because the bonus creates no value [S7, F38, F41].

Related-party dealings are present but small at the operating line. The company pays charter hire to a related party at market rates, and the interim report discloses a service fee to IMC Industrial Pte Ltd of US$0.2m in the nine months to September 2026, which is a small share of operating expenses, and other payables to related parties of US$1.6m, a small share of total liabilities [S3, F19, F44]. The charter-hire amount itself is not separately quantified in the related-party note, so we cannot state it as a share of cost of revenue; the pricing policy is disclosed as market-based, and we treat the flow as an unquantified governance discount rather than a valuation input [S3]. The directors' fee line of US$1.3m in FY2025 is high relative to net profit and to the size of the company, and it is a recurring governance cost that a minority holder should note [S2].

The auditor is Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, the Indonesian member firm of Ernst & Young, and the FY2025 opinion is unqualified: the accounts present fairly, in all material respects, in accordance with Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S2]. We found no qualification, emphasis-of-matter or going-concern paragraph in the opinion we read [S2]. The dividend record is real but shrinking with the cycle: the company paid US$1.4m out of FY2025 profit, a lower amount than in the stronger years, and the policy caps distribution at a share of net profit [S2, F26]. The board is led by a president director and a finance director, with independent commissioners in place; we did not find a board-level governance event in the period [S2].

ESG exposures are the standard shipping set. The company reports fleet fuel efficiency measures, including engine power limitation and biofuel trials, and says it recorded no safety incidents in the reporting year [S2]. Emissions are direct combustion emissions from vessel fuel, and the main transition risk is the cost of compliance and fleet renewal rather than a demand shock within our horizon [S2]. The social exposure is crew welfare and community programmes, which are small relative to the cost base. The governance exposure is the concentrated ownership, the thin float and the related-party charter arrangement; none of these is manipulation-class, but they justify the discount the market applies [S2, S3].

The near-term catalyst is the treasury-share bonus: it went ex on 6 November 2026, the record date is 9 November 2026 and the distribution follows on 27 November 2026, with the share count rising by 172.0m and ownership percentages unchanged [S7, S9]. The FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 are the next hard data point; we will compare the full-year gross margin, the capex cash flow and the net cash balance against the nine-month run-rate [S2, S3]. The annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision follow under the stated policy [S2]. The 2027 RKAB quota approval is the main swing factor for customer volumes and therefore for barge demand [S2]. The renewal programme's delivery schedule and the utilisation of the new barges are the operational proof of the capex thesis [S5].

Between updates we watch the KPIs that matter: the quarterly gross margin, because it is the cleanest read on the tariff-cost spread; revenue per unit of fleet, because it separates utilisation from tariff; capex and the net cash balance, because the renewal is the largest discretionary use of cash; and the related-party and directors' fee disclosures, because they are the governance costs that do not show up in EBITDA [S2, S3]. A sustained improvement in the first two without a deterioration in the last two would move us toward the bull case; the reverse would move us toward the bear. The single signpost we would act on fastest is a board commitment to return excess cash: at the current discount to book it would change the arithmetic without needing a margin recovery [S3].

bear.narrative: RKAB quotas and customer production stay weak, the oversupplied barge market keeps tariffs flat, the six new vessels fail to fill or arrive late, and fuel stays high enough to eat the spread. The renewal slips into FY2028 on yard delays, so the group pays for the old and the new fleet at once and the capex charge runs above the base case for the forecast; the fleet earns below its cost of capital through the forecast, and the coal transition caps long-run growth below the house terminal rate.

bull.narrative: Coal output normalises as the price eases toward the deck path, tariffs recover from the 2026 trough, the new barges fill quickly, and the market closes part of the book-value discount as free cash flow turns positive and the excess cash is returned.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 revenue was US$35.1m against US$44.5m a year earlier, so FY2026E is anchored to the nine-month actual annualised (about US$46.8m) plus a small fourth-quarter uplift, rather than to a price forecast; the interim accounts carry no quarterly split, so we do not read a sequential pattern into them. FY2027E grows 5% as six new vessels join the fleet. The six-vessel programme is a renewal, not a net expansion: the fleet fell from 52 vessels in FY2024 to 48 at end-FY2025 and 47 at September 2026 as older tonnage was sold, and S5 describes the new tugs and barges as reliability and flexibility for customers, with delivery staged by market conditions [S2, S5, F8, F28]. Growth then eases to 4%, 3% and 3% as the coal trade normalises on the deck path (Newcastle FY2027E 118 against FY2026E 137); long-run 3% tracks fleet capacity [S2, S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The nine-month 2026 gross margin was 10.3% on US$35.1m of revenue, after a 9.6% FY2025 that management attributes to tariff pressure and fleet oversupply. The 11.3% base-input margin is that actual grossed back up for the oil link's own arithmetic: the model reprices fuel at the FY2026E deck Brent of 96.0 against the FY2025 deck average of 68.1 [deck], and with fuel at 23.5% of cost of revenue and 30% of the move unpassed (a.link2_pass 0.70, F20, F60) that adds about 2.5pp of margin, while the 1.2% final shipping levy moved into operating costs takes about 0.9pp back; a +1.7pp base-margin offset and a 0.9pp D&A ratio then leave the modelled FY2026E gross margin about 1.5pp below the nine-month actual and the EBITDA-margin calibration gap at -2.7pp [S2, S3, deck]. That de-linking is arithmetic, not a change of view. We let it recover to 19.0% by FY2030E, below the 26.1% FY2024 and 36.8% FY2023 actuals, but we do not hold absolute COGS flat: fuel (23.5% of COGS, F20) and charter hire (16.1%, F21) are roughly 40% of the cost base and are variable with volume, so a revenue path driven by new vessels carries incremental fuel and charter cost. The resulting margin path is the 11.3% starting level compounded by a 40%-variable cost base, not the flat-COGS 20% path that a pure price-recovery assumption would imply [S2, S3, S5, F20, F21].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal is the cargo, not an input: cost of revenue is depreciation, fuel, charter hire, crew, repairs, port and insurance charges, with no coal purchase line, so the Newcastle deck carries no direct cost exposure and the coal cycle is held in revenue_growth instead [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: With no coal line in cost of revenue the pass-through parameter is set to zero; the coal price affects the business through freight demand and tariff renegotiation, which the revenue path already carries [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel and diesel oil of US$12.16m was 23.5% of the US$51.63m cost of revenue in FY2025, the only material oil-linked input line [S2, F20, F22].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Measured, not asserted. In the nine months to September 2026 fuel was US$9.43m on revenue of US$35.10m, 26.9%, against US$10.37m on US$44.50m, 23.3%, a year earlier: fuel intensity rose 3.6pp while Brent rose about 41% over FY2025 [S3, F58, F59]. With fuel at roughly a fifth of revenue, a zero-pass-through world would have added about 8pp of intensity, so the realised recovery is close to 55-60%. We round up to 70% because part of the intensity rise is volume deleveraging on fewer tonnes per voyage rather than a pass-through failure, and because the medium-term time-charter contracts carry tariff reset clauses [S2, S3, F58, F59]. The previous 90% was unsourced and is withdrawn.

assumptions.label: SG&A plus final shipping tax / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were US$6.11m, 10.70% of revenue, in FY2025 and US$3.77m, 10.73% of revenue, in the nine months to September 2026 [S2, S3]. On top of that the company pays the 1.2% final shipping tax on vessel-operation and charter revenue (Note 32c): at 9M2026 the US$0.321m final tax was 0.92% of total revenue and was charged even though the pre-final-tax result was a loss [S3, F43]. It is a revenue levy that must reduce cash before CIT, but the engine's FCFF formula carries only a profit tax, so we include the levy in operating costs: 10.7% + 0.9% = 11.6%. CIT is then 20% on the residual. Reported EBITDA is therefore after the levy and not directly comparable with the pre-levy history, which is disclosed in section 3 [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of fixed assets was US$12.81m in FY2025, 22.4% of revenue, and US$7.45m in the nine months to September 2026, about 21.4% of the annualised run-rate; held at 21.5% as the renewal fleet enters service [S2, S3, F3].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was US$15.55m in the nine months to September 2026 against US$9.60m in FY2025, as the six-vessel renewal programme is paid for [S2, S3, F5, F12]. FY2026E is set at 40% of revenue, the actual run-rate. FY2027E falls to 20% to allow for the staged delivery described in S5 (no delivery schedule or remaining contract value is disclosed, so this is an estimate, not a commitment). FY2028E-FY2030E are held at the FY2025 actual 17% ratio while the renewed fleet is young; from FY2031E the long-run ratio rises to 21.5% of revenue, equal to the depreciation charge, because a perpetual 2% growth business cannot invest below its depreciation charge indefinitely. The earlier flat 17% long-run ratio added roughly two-fifths of terminal FCFF from under-investment [S2, S3, S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Trade receivables, contract assets and inventories less trade and other payables were US$6.45m at December 2025, 11.3% of sales; the September 2026 balance sheet repeats the same order of magnitude, so the ratio is held at the last actual [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The company pays a 1.2% final tax on shipping revenue plus corporate income tax; the FY2024 effective rate was 13.9% and FY2023 11.1%, so 20% is a prudent blend of the final-tax wedge and the 22% statutory rate rather than the distorted 83.6% FY2025 print caused by a near-zero pre-tax base [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of US$0.61m in the nine months to September 2026 on about US$10m of opening bank debt and leases annualise to roughly 8%, the effective rate on the Multiarta Sentosa term loan [S3].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of US$0.55m in the nine months to September 2026 on more than US$60m of cash, deposits and funds is a low single-digit yield; 1.5% is the observed run-rate [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The bank term loan is amortising and the company carries large net cash; the model holds debt flat rather than assume new borrowing [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The non-controlling interest is small and concentrated in subsidiaries such as the 63.16%-owned property entity; 5% of consolidated net profit is the observed share [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The stated policy is a distribution of up to a maximum of 30% of net profit [S2, F26]. The company has paid above the cap in cash-rich years - 41% for FY2022, 40% for FY2023 and a 95% interim for FY2024 - but with net profit near zero in the forecast the cash return is dominated by the balance sheet, not the payout ratio, so the policy cap is the repeatable anchor and the excess-cash distribution is treated as a scenario in sections 4 and 5 [S2, F49, F50, F51].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The 30:1 bonus transfers 172.04m treasury shares to holders, so outstanding shares rise from the 5,161.2m distribution base to 5,333.2m on the 6 November 2026 ex-date; total issued shares are unchanged and the transfer is pro rata, so no holder's percentage changes. The engine's share count is restated from the bs_shares fact (F38, 5,161.2m) and the shares line from F55, so the target and every per-share figure are struck on the cum-bonus base of the Rp336 close, not grown through this input, which is therefore zero. On the post-bonus count the target is proportionately lower and the return is unchanged [S3, S7, F27, F38, F41, F42, F55].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the US-dollar reporting currency; Indonesian coal distribution volumes are flat-to-slow-growing, so the standard 2% is used [S2].

challenges.challenge: The rating is produced by the liquidity discount, not by the valuation. The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp333.13 and the price is Rp336.00, so on the report's own numbers the fundamental expected return is -0.9% before discounting; the entire -20.7% comes from applying a 20% ADTV haircut to intrinsic value while leaving the market price, which is itself the price of that same illiquid stock, unadjusted. That double-counts illiquidity and it is the single input that separates REDUCE from HOLD. Section 4 says the discount is "not an analyst choice" and moves on, and the investment summary attributes the rating to the 13.5%-vs-5.0% recovery instead.
challenges.answer: Accepted and disclosed, with the economics re-struck so the rating no longer rests on an undisclosed haircut. The engine values the probability-weighted business at Rp305 before the haircut against the Rp336 price; the summary now says so in its own paragraph, states that the haircut alone separates the rating from HOLD, and the thesis bullet carries both numbers. We also rebut the double-count framing with evidence: the constitution's ladder is a fund exit constraint (ADTV below the Rp500m floor), applied to every name below the floor and shown as its own line rather than folded into WACC, so it measures what our own position can be sold for, not a second guess at the stock's price. The fundamental side of the case was also strengthened independently: with the EV/EBITDA leg zero-weighted and a measured fuel pass-through, the undiscounted value is Rp305 against the Rp336 close, inside the HOLD band but no longer a coin toss.

challenges.challenge: The largest cost event in the interim accounts is not in the report. Charter hire fell to US$2.96m in 9M2026 from US$6.45m in 9M2025 (-54%) [S3 Note 26], an annualised US$3.95m against the US$8.30m FY2025 figure the report still quotes [F21]. That is ~US$4.3m of annual cost relief, ~9pp of gross margin on the FY2026E revenue base, and it sits directly under the recovery from 10.4% to 18.8% gross margin that carries the DCF. Whether it is a permanent cut or a response to lower volume changes the whole margin path.
challenges.answer: The charter-hire collapse is now in the file with its source. Facts F58 and F59 take the nine-month figures from Note 26 (US$2.96m against US$6.45m), and section 3 states the annualised run-rate, compares it with the FY2025 charge, and classifies the cut as structural - chartered-in tonnage falling as the owned renewal fleet arrives - while noting the mirror risk that it is volume-driven and reverses with the 2027 RKAB cycle. The base-case margin path already starts from the nine-month actual, so the relief is inside the forecast rather than added on top; the paragraph says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: Revenue per vessel is assumed never to recover. On the report's own inputs revenue per vessel falls from US$1.19m in FY2025 (US$57.10m/48) to US$0.95m in FY2027E (US$50.37m on 53 vessels after the six-new-barge programme in which each barge carries more than 10,000t [S5, F29]) and reaches only US$1.22m in FY2035E. A younger, larger fleet earning 20% less per vessel than the FY2025 downcycle for a decade is a default haircut, and no source or argument supports it.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states the fleet arithmetic behind unit revenue: 52 vessels at end-FY2024, 48 at end-FY2025 and 47 at September 2026 as older tonnage was sold, with the six new tugs and barges a renewal of that capacity rather than an addition, so their revenue is not stacked on top of the existing fleet and single-digit revenue growth on a larger hull count leaves unit revenue below FY2025. We state plainly that the retirement schedule and the per-tonne tariff are not disclosed, that the path is a judgement rather than a sourced number, and that a reader who believes the renewed barges earn the legacy rate should hold the bull case, where that recovery is. We have not lifted the FY2027E growth assumption on an unsourced unit-revenue recovery.

challenges.challenge: The DCF values the operating business at a US$28.51m EV - 0.36x the US$80.12m fleet net book value [F39] and 2.3x trough EBITDA - while US$49m of net cash and financial assets sits idle at a 1.2-1.5% yield against a 12.36% cost of equity. Section 4 calls a special dividend or buyback "the main upside risk to our target" and says a buyback at a discount to book would be accretive, but no scenario models one: the bull case's Rp495 comes purely from +6pp revenue growth and +3.5pp gross margin and leaves the US$49m untouched. The company paid 95% of profit as an interim in FY2024 [F51].
challenges.answer: A fourth scenario would double count cash we already count. The net cash and financial assets are added to equity value at face value in the bridge, so distributing half of them moves value from the company to the holder and leaves value per share unchanged: the variant would show the same target with a different holder mix, not a different value. A buyback is worse than neutral at today's price, and we have corrected the report's claim that it would be accretive: at the close the company would repurchase above our intrinsic value, which transfers value from continuing holders to sellers. The FY2024 interim at 95 per cent of profit and the above-policy payouts show willingness but are discretionary and family-controlled [F26, F49, F50, F51], so they belong in the signposts, not in a probability-weighted scenario we would have to assign a probability to.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not stress the one discretionary commitment that can break the balance-sheet floor. Capex runs US$19.19m in FY2026E and US$10.07m in FY2027E against FCFF of -US$8.16m and +US$1.01m [model], and the report itself flags "renewal capex extends into FY2027 or FY2028, or new vessels fail to fill" as a medium-likelihood, high-impact risk. The bear shock set is only revenue growth -6pp, gross margin -3.5pp, WACC +1pp, g -1pp, which leaves capex and the cash bridge exactly as modelled.
challenges.answer: The bear now stresses capex as well as the operating case. The shock set adds a capex ratio widening (mirrored in the bull by an equal narrowing), the narrative describes the renewal slipping into FY2028 so the group carries the old and new fleet at once, and the bear value falls from Rp249 to Rp200 in the re-run - the cash bridge and the operating case are cut together, as required. The scenario table and the section 5 text are rebuilt around the new bear.

challenges.challenge: The fuel pass-through is asserted, not measured. link2_pass is 90% on FY2025 fuel of US$12.16m at 23.5% of COGS [F20, F22], but 9M2026 fuel of US$9.43m on revenue of US$35.10m is 26.9% of revenue against 23.3% in 9M2025 [S3], so fuel intensity rose 3.6pp in the downcycle - the opposite of full pass-through when volumes fall. Section 2 nonetheless says "the nine-month 2026 result shows the mechanism working in the other direction as fuel costs normalised", which that source does not support, and the qc justification cites a 41% 2026 Brent spike.
challenges.answer: Measured rather than asserted. Fuel was US$9.43m on US$35.10m of revenue in 9M2026 against US$10.37m on US$44.50m in 9M2025, so intensity rose from 23.3 to 26.9 per cent, about 3.6pp, while Brent rose roughly 41 per cent over FY2025; with fuel near a fifth of revenue, zero pass-through would have added about 8pp of intensity, implying a realised recovery near 55-60 per cent. We set link2_pass at 70 per cent, rounding up for the volume-deleveraging component that is not a pass-through failure, and state that the previous 90 per cent was unsourced and withdrawn. challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check keeps 15% weight on a multiple the report knows is wrong.
